The parts of ruststream-rumqttc an MQTT service uses, one page per component: the broker (MqttBroker), its subscriptions, its publish policy and the in-process transport a TestApp test runs on. The broker pages cover its connection, session, last will, limits, startup and shutdown. The subscriptions read a topic or a filter with wildcards, with its quality of service and share group, overlapping filters and batches. Settlement is what each handler outcome sends on MQTT, with retries, the attempt cap and dead-letter topics. The context carries the topic a delivery was published to. Publishing covers the publish policy, the quality of service and retain flag of one message, headers and responders. The AsyncAPI pages show the mqtt bindings of the generated document. Testing runs the production app on an in-process MQTT server, and the same test against a running one.

With the asyncapi feature the generated document speaks MQTT 5: the session the client opens, the QoS of each operation and the properties of each message. The core builds the AsyncAPI document from the app, before anything connects. This crate adds the specification's mqtt binding, version 0.2.0, to the parts it knows about. A server reports where the client connects, the protocol version 5 and the session it opens. An operation reports the quality of service it runs at. A message reports the MQTT 5 properties it rides. A reply named per request reports where its address is read. Everything comes from the service's own declarations: the broker, the descriptors, the publish policies and the transforms. The document is published and shared, so no binding carries a credential. The binary #[ruststream::app] writes prints the document with asyncapi gen.

The dependency line: ruststream-rumqttc = { version = "0.7", features = ["asyncapi"] } The service registers its broker under the label mqtt, the key of its server in the document. cargo run --example mqtt_asyncapi --features asyncapi -- asyncapi gen prints the document. Macros Manual examples/mqtt_asyncapi.rs fn service(broker: MqttBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("telemetry", "1.0.0")).with_broker_labeled("mqtt", broker, |b| { b.include(collect) .out(Alerts, Publish::default().retain(true)) .out_retry(Publish::default()) .to("devices/retry/telemetry") .build(); b.include(answer) .out_reply(Publish::default()) .transform(ToResponseTopic); }) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { let password = env::var("MQTT_PASSWORD").unwrap_or_default(); service(broker(&password)) } examples/manual/mqtt_asyncapi.rs fn service(broker: MqttBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("telemetry", "1.0.0")).with_broker_labeled("mqtt", broker, |b| { b.include( subscriber("devices/+/telemetry", Collect) .build() .map_source(|_| fleet()), ) .out(Alerts, Publish::default().retain(true)) .out_retry(Publish::default()) .to("devices/retry/telemetry") .build(); // A request without a response topic is answered on `devices/dev42/pong`. let answer = subscriber("devices/dev42/ping", Answer) .map_source(|_| MqttTopic::new("devices/dev42/ping")); b.include(answer.reply().to("devices/dev42/pong").build()) .out_reply(Publish::default()) .transform(ToResponseTopic); }) } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { let password = env::var("MQTT_PASSWORD").unwrap_or_default(); service(broker(&password)) }

Each message reports the MQTT 5 properties it rides: a delivery the response topic and correlation data, a published message the correlation data. The crate carries two headers in the protocol's own properties: correlation-id in Correlation Data and reply-to in Response Topic. The message binding describes them, each as a string. A message a subscription reads reports both. A requester sets the response topic on its own request, and a message a service publishes is not that request. So a message an Out slot or a reply sends reports the correlation data alone. Where a reply goes is the operation's reply object, and a reply named per request reports its address there. The payload format indicator stays out of the binding. It follows the media type one message carries in its content-type header, which no declaration knows. The document reports the media type of the position's codec in the contentType the core fills.

Telemetry reports correlationData and responseTopic; Alert, which the slot publishes, reports correlationData only. Macros Manual examples/mqtt_asyncapi.rs /// What every device publishes; a subscription reads it. #[derive(Debug, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] struct Telemetry { device: String, temperature: f64, } /// What the service publishes through its slot when a device runs hot. #[derive(Debug, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "alerts/overheat")] struct Alert { device: String, } examples/manual/mqtt_asyncapi.rs /// What every device publishes; a subscription reads it. #[derive(Debug, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Telemetry { device: String, temperature: f64, } /// What the service publishes through its slot when a device runs hot. #[derive(Debug, Serialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] #[outgoing(name = "alerts/overheat")] struct Alert { device: String, }

A receive operation reports the QoS its subscription reads at; a send operation reports the QoS and retain flag of its policy. The operation binding carries qos, the level as a number: 0, 1 or 2. A receive operation takes it from the descriptor's qos. A share group is part of the subscribed filter and adds nothing to the binding. A send operation comes from an Out slot or a dead-letter topic. It reports both arguments of the PUBLISH packet its publish policy declares: qos and retain. A reply has no send operation of its own, so a reply policy adds nothing to the document's operations.

The operation receive_devices___telemetry reports { "qos": 2 }. The slot's operation send_devices___telemetry_alerts_overheat reports { "qos": 1, "retain": true }, from the policy Publish::default().retain(true) the app attaches. Macros Manual examples/mqtt_asyncapi.rs /// Reads the fleet at `QoS` 2 as a member of `workers`, and raises an alert through its slot. #[subscriber(MqttFilter::new("devices/+/telemetry").qos(Qos::ExactlyOnce).shared("workers"))] async fn collect( telemetry: &Telemetry, Out(alerts): Out<impl Publisher, Alerts>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { if telemetry.temperature > 30.0 { let alert = Alert { device: telemetry.device.clone(), }; if let Err(err) = alerts.message(&alert).publish().await { tracing::warn!(subscription = "devices/+/telemetry", error = %err, "alert not published"); return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/mqtt_asyncapi.rs /// The fleet, read at `QoS` 2 as a member of `workers`. fn fleet() -> MqttFilter { MqttFilter::new("devices/+/telemetry") .qos(Qos::ExactlyOnce) .shared("workers") }

A reply named per request has no fixed channel, so the document points its address at the reply-to header of the request. A responder answers on the response topic its request carries. The crate maps that property onto the reply-to header, and a publish transform with Destination = Names reads it there. The document is built before any request arrives, so it cannot name the topic. The operation's reply.address.location is $message.header#/reply-to instead: a client reads the address of its answer from the header of its own request. The mount-site name, reply("devices/dev42/pong"), is the reply channel the document reports, and where a request without a response topic is answered. A reply that the type or the mount site names reports that channel alone.

The operation receive_devices_dev42_ping reports "location": "$message.header#/reply-to" in its reply address. Macros Manual examples/mqtt_asyncapi.rs /// Answers on the topic the request names in its response topic, the `reply-to` header. struct ToResponseTopic; impl<C, Options> PublishTransform<ForReply<C>, Options> for ToResponseTopic { type Destination = Names; fn apply( &self, out: &mut Outgoing<'_>, _options: &mut Option<Options>, cx: &PublishContext<'_, C>, ) { if let Some(topic) = cx.headers().get_str("reply-to") { out.set_name(topic.to_owned()); } } } /// A request without a response topic is answered on `devices/dev42/pong`. #[subscriber(MqttTopic::new("devices/dev42/ping"), reply("devices/dev42/pong"))] async fn answer(ping: &Telemetry) -> Pong { Pong { device: ping.device.clone(), } } examples/manual/mqtt_asyncapi.rs /// Answers on the topic the request names in its response topic, the `reply-to` header. struct ToResponseTopic; impl<C, Options> PublishTransform<ForReply<C>, Options> for ToResponseTopic { type Destination = Names; fn apply( &self, out: &mut Outgoing<'_>, _options: &mut Option<Options>, cx: &PublishContext<'_, C>, ) { if let Some(topic) = cx.headers().get_str("reply-to") { out.set_name(topic.to_owned()); } } }

The server reports host and port with MQTT 5 and the session binding: client id, clean start, keep-alive, expiry, last will, never credentials. A broker registered with with_broker_labeled is a server of the document, under its label. Its host is the host and port of the broker's URL. A URL without a port reports the protocol's default: 1883 for mqtt://, 8883 for mqtts://. The protocol is mqtt and the protocolVersion is 5, the only version the crate speaks. The server binding describes the session the client opens. clientId is the client id of MqttBroker::new, and maximumPacketSize is the packet limit, 1 MiB by default. cleanSession, keepAlive and sessionExpiryInterval appear when the broker sets clean_start, keep_alive and session_expiry. lastWill reports the last will's topic, quality of service and retain flag. The will's payload is the content of a message, so it stays out. The user name and password of credentials stay out too.

The broker logs in, keeps its session for an hour and leaves a last will. Its server in the document is mqtt.internal:1883, with the session below and no password. { "bindingVersion": "0.2.0", "clientId": "telemetry-svc", "cleanSession": false, "keepAlive": 30, "sessionExpiryInterval": 3600, "maximumPacketSize": 1048576, "lastWill": { "topic": "devices/svc/status", "qos": 1, "retain": true } } Macros Manual examples/mqtt_asyncapi.rs /// The production server, with a persistent session and a last will. fn broker(password: &str) -> MqttBroker { MqttBroker::new("mqtt://mqtt.internal:1883", "telemetry-svc") .credentials("telemetry-svc", password) .keep_alive(Duration::from_secs(30)) .clean_start(false) .session_expiry(Duration::from_hours(1)) .last_will( "devices/svc/status", b"offline".to_vec(), Qos::AtLeastOnce, true, ) } examples/manual/mqtt_asyncapi.rs /// The production server, with a persistent session and a last will. fn broker(password: &str) -> MqttBroker { MqttBroker::new("mqtt://mqtt.internal:1883", "telemetry-svc") .credentials("telemetry-svc", password) .keep_alive(Duration::from_secs(30)) .clean_start(false) .session_expiry(Duration::from_hours(1)) .last_will( "devices/svc/status", b"offline".to_vec(), Qos::AtLeastOnce, true, ) }

MqttBroker connects a service to an MQTT 5 server; new only records the URL and the client id, and the runtime connects it at startup. MqttBroker::new takes the server's URL, mqtt://host:port or mqtts://host:port, and the client id. A URL without a port takes 1883, or 8883 for mqtts://. It does no I/O, so the whole service fits the synchronous #[ruststream::app] builder. The settings that follow it are builder steps too: credentials and TLS, the session, the last will, the limits, the reconnect mode and the keep-alive. Each page gives the default a setting has when the service leaves it unset. The client id is the session's identity on the server. A second connection under the same id takes the session over, and the server closes the first one. So two instances of one service connect under two ids, and share their work through a share group. At startup the runtime connects the broker and receives a ConnectedMqttBroker. The crate runs one task per connection: it drives the client's event loop, hands each delivery to its subscription, and reconnects when the connection is lost. Every subscription and every publisher of the service shares that connection. At shutdown the runtime closes it with a clean DISCONNECT. #[subscriber("devices/dev42/telemetry")] reads one topic at QoS 1. A MqttFilter reads many topics through the + and # wildcards, and the other descriptors are on the Subscriptions pages. The crate speaks MQTT 5 only: headers ride its user properties, and share groups exist only there. The crate has two features, both off by default. testing adds the in-process mode a TestApp test connects, and asyncapi adds the MQTT bindings of the generated document. The codec is the service's choice: json, msgpack or cbor on ruststream itself.

The service reads the telemetry of every device in the share group workers. A filter names no topic a retry copy could go to, so the mount site names one. cargo run --example mqtt_service --features testing -- run starts it against a server on localhost:1883. Macros Manual examples/mqtt_service.rs use ruststream_rumqttc::prelude::*; #[subscriber(MqttFilter::new("devices/+/telemetry").shared("workers"))] async fn record(telemetry: &Telemetry) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(telemetry.device, telemetry.temperature, "reading recorded"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("telemetry", "0.1.0")).with_broker( MqttBroker::new("mqtt://localhost:1883", "telemetry-svc"), |b| { // A filter matches many topics and names none of them, so the mount site says where // a retry copy is published. b.include(record) .out_retry(Publish::default()) .to("devices/retry/telemetry"); }, ) } examples/manual/mqtt_service.rs use ruststream_rumqttc::prelude::*; struct Record; impl Handle<Telemetry> for Record { fn handle( &self, telemetry: &Telemetry, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(telemetry.device, telemetry.temperature, "reading recorded"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn telemetry() -> MqttFilter { MqttFilter::new("devices/+/telemetry").shared("workers") } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("telemetry", "0.1.0")).with_broker( MqttBroker::new("mqtt://localhost:1883", "telemetry-svc"), |b| { let record = subscriber("devices/+/telemetry", Record).map_source(|_| telemetry()); // A filter matches many topics and names none of them, so the mount site says where // a retry copy is published. b.include(record.build()) .out_retry(Publish::default()) .to("devices/retry/telemetry"); }, ) }

MqttError is the one error type of the crate: the connect, a subscription, a delivery, a publish, a closed connection and an invalid setting. Each variant names the step that failed. The client's errors become text inside it, so the rumqttc types stay out of the crate's API. Variant When Connect the server refused the connection, the TLS handshake failed, or no CONNACK came within 30 seconds Subscribe the server rejected a filter, or the connection ended while a subscription opened Receive the connection ended for good: the server refused it for a reason no retry changes, or the reconnect mode gave up Publish the topic is not one a server takes (empty, with a wildcard or a control character), a header has no MQTT form, or the connection task is gone NotConnected a publisher was used, or a subscription opened, after the broker shut down Invalid a setting or a descriptor cannot work, such as a keep-alive under five seconds or a share group with a / A service meets the error in two places. A failed startup carries it as the source of the runtime's error, and the service exits before it reads anything. A publish from a handler returns it inside the core's PublishError, and the handler decides how the delivery settles. The enum is #[non_exhaustive], so a match on it ends with a wildcard arm.

An alert goes to the topic of its device. A device id with a wildcard makes no topic, so the handler logs the refusal and drops the reading: a retry would fail the same way. Macros Manual examples/mqtt_broker_errors.rs #[subscriber("broker-errors/telemetry")] async fn check(telemetry: &Telemetry, Out(alerts): Out<impl Publisher>) -> HandlerOutcome { if telemetry.temperature <= 30.0 { return HandlerOutcome::ack(); } let alert = Alert { temperature: telemetry.temperature, }; let topic = format!("alerts/{}", telemetry.device); if let Err(err) = alerts.message(&alert).to(&topic).publish().await { // A device id with `+` or `#` makes no topic, and no retry changes that. tracing::warn!( subscription = "broker-errors/telemetry", device = telemetry.device, error = %err, "alert not published" ); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/mqtt_broker_errors.rs struct Check; impl<Entry> Handle<Telemetry, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Check where Entry: OutEntry<DefaultSlot, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, telemetry: &Telemetry, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { if telemetry.temperature <= 30.0 { return Ok(()); } let alert = Alert { temperature: telemetry.temperature, }; let topic = format!("alerts/{}", telemetry.device); if let Err(err) = outs .get(DefaultSlot) .message(&alert) .to(&topic) .publish() .await { // A device id with `+` or `#` makes no topic, and no retry changes that. tracing::warn!( subscription = "broker-errors/telemetry", device = telemetry.device, error = %err, "alert not published" ); return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); } Ok(()) } }

last_will names the message the server publishes when the connection ends without a clean disconnect, such as a service's offline status. The will travels in the CONNECT packet, and the server keeps it for as long as the connection lasts. It has a topic, a payload, a QoS and a retain flag, like any publish. The payload is bytes, written as the service's readers decode them; no codec runs on it. The server publishes the will when the connection ends any other way than by the client's DISCONNECT. That covers a process that dies, a network that drops, a connection silent past its keep-alive, and a second client that takes the client id over. A clean shutdown sends a DISCONNECT, and the server discards the will. A retained will stays on its topic, so a dashboard that subscribes later still reads that the service is gone. The server publishes the will, so a TestApp test in process runs the app without it. A live test shows it. The generated AsyncAPI document reports the will's topic, QoS and retain flag, not its payload.

Each instance announces its own death on services/<client id>/status, retained. Macros Manual examples/mqtt_broker_last_will.rs /// If the connection ends without a clean disconnect, the server publishes `{"online":false}` /// on the service's status topic and keeps it there for every later subscriber. fn broker(url: &str, client_id: &str) -> MqttBroker { MqttBroker::new(url, client_id).last_will( format!("services/{client_id}/status"), r#"{"online":false}"#, Qos::AtLeastOnce, true, ) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(broker("mqtt://localhost:1883", "telemetry-svc")) } examples/manual/mqtt_broker_last_will.rs /// If the connection ends without a clean disconnect, the server publishes `{"online":false}` /// on the service's status topic and keeps it there for every later subscriber. fn broker(url: &str, client_id: &str) -> MqttBroker { MqttBroker::new(url, client_id).last_will( format!("services/{client_id}/status"), r#"{"online":false}"#, Qos::AtLeastOnce, true, ) } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(broker("mqtt://localhost:1883", "telemetry-svc")) }

max_packet_size caps what the server may send, 1 MiB by default; receive_maximum caps unacknowledged QoS 1 and 2 deliveries, 1000 by default. Both travel to the server in the CONNECT packet, and the server holds itself to them. Both take a non-zero type, NonZeroU32 and NonZeroU16, because a server refuses a session that announces a zero limit. A constant such as const IN_FLIGHT: NonZeroU16 = NonZeroU16::new(100).unwrap(); is checked when the service compiles. A message larger than max_packet_size never reaches the service: the server drops it for this client and delivers it to everyone else. The rumqttc client alone would allow 10 KiB and close the connection on a larger packet, so the crate raises its default to 1 MiB. A service whose payloads are larger raises it to fit them. receive_maximum is MQTT's flow control. The server sends QoS 1 and 2 deliveries until that many wait for an acknowledgement, then holds the rest until one is settled. So it also bounds what queues up in front of a slow handler. A delivery left unacknowledged holds its place until the connection ends: HandlerOutcome::retry(), for one, acknowledges nothing. Once every place is held, the server delivers no QoS 1 or 2 message on the connection, to any subscription, until the connection ends. QoS 0 deliveries need no acknowledgement and are not bounded. A TestApp test in process drops a message over max_packet_size as the server does. The window lives on the server, so it is for a live test.

Firmware images reach 256 KiB, and at most 100 deliveries wait for an acknowledgement. Macros Manual examples/mqtt_broker_limits.rs const LARGEST_PACKET: NonZeroU32 = NonZeroU32::new(256 * 1024).unwrap(); const IN_FLIGHT: NonZeroU16 = NonZeroU16::new(100).unwrap(); /// Firmware images reach 256 KiB, and at most 100 deliveries wait for an acknowledgement. fn broker(url: &str, client_id: &str) -> MqttBroker { MqttBroker::new(url, client_id) .max_packet_size(LARGEST_PACKET) .receive_maximum(IN_FLIGHT) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(broker("mqtt://localhost:1883", "firmware-svc")) } examples/manual/mqtt_broker_limits.rs const LARGEST_PACKET: NonZeroU32 = NonZeroU32::new(256 * 1024).unwrap(); const IN_FLIGHT: NonZeroU16 = NonZeroU16::new(100).unwrap(); /// Firmware images reach 256 KiB, and at most 100 deliveries wait for an acknowledgement. fn broker(url: &str, client_id: &str) -> MqttBroker { MqttBroker::new(url, client_id) .max_packet_size(LARGEST_PACKET) .receive_maximum(IN_FLIGHT) } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(broker("mqtt://localhost:1883", "firmware-svc")) }

One glob, ruststream_rumqttc::prelude, brings the core prelude, the descriptors, Qos, the policy as Publish and the context key. use ruststream_rumqttc::prelude::*; is the one import a routes file on MQTT writes. It carries the core's own prelude, so #[subscriber], RustStream, HandlerOutcome and Out come with it. It adds MqttBroker, the descriptors MqttTopic and MqttFilter, their quality of service Qos, and the context type MqttContext with its key DeliveryTopic. The publish policy comes under the name every broker crate uses: Publish is MqttPublish. So a mount site reads the same on every broker. Two broker preludes in one file collide on that name; the prefixed MqttPublish at the crate root tells them apart. A handler body bounds its slots with capability traits, such as Out<impl Publisher>, and names no broker type. So a file of handlers imports ruststream::prelude::* alone. The one exception is a body that sets the QoS or the retain flag of one message: it needs MqttPublishSteps in scope and the slot bounded Out<impl Publisher<Options = MqttPublishOptions>, Marker>, both from this prelude. MqttError is named where it is handled, from the crate root.

The descriptor, its QoS, the context key and the policy all come from the one glob. Macros Manual examples/mqtt_broker_prelude.rs use ruststream_rumqttc::prelude::*; #[subscriber(MqttFilter::new("devices/+/telemetry").qos(Qos::AtLeastOnce))] async fn check( telemetry: &Telemetry, Ctx(topic): Ctx<DeliveryTopic>, Out(alerts): Out<impl Publisher>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { if telemetry.temperature <= 30.0 { return HandlerOutcome::ack(); } if alerts.message(&Alert { topic }).publish().await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("telemetry", "0.1.0")).with_broker( MqttBroker::new("mqtt://localhost:1883", "telemetry-svc"), |b| { b.include(check) .out(DefaultSlot, Publish::default().qos(Qos::ExactlyOnce)) .out_retry(Publish::default()) .to("devices/retry/telemetry") .build(); }, ) } examples/manual/mqtt_broker_prelude.rs use ruststream_rumqttc::prelude::*; struct Check; impl<Entry> Handle<Telemetry, (), Outs<(Entry,)>, MqttContext> for Check where Entry: OutEntry<DefaultSlot, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, telemetry: &Telemetry, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, ctx: &mut Context<'_, MqttContext>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { if telemetry.temperature <= 30.0 { return Ok(()); } let alert = Alert { topic: ctx.context(DeliveryTopic).to_owned(), }; if outs .get(DefaultSlot) .message(&alert) .publish() .await .is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(()) } } fn telemetry() -> MqttFilter { MqttFilter::new("devices/+/telemetry").qos(Qos::AtLeastOnce) } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("telemetry", "0.1.0")).with_broker( MqttBroker::new("mqtt://localhost:1883", "telemetry-svc"), |b| { let check = subscriber("devices/+/telemetry", Check).map_source(|_| telemetry()); b.include(check.build()) .out(DefaultSlot, Publish::default().qos(Qos::ExactlyOnce)) .out_retry(Publish::default()) .to("devices/retry/telemetry") .build(); }, ) }

reconnect chooses what a connection lost after startup does: the client dials again by default, and a service may choose no reconnection or one of its own. A connection ends when the server closes it, sends a DISCONNECT (a restart, a keep-alive that ran out), or stops answering. Three modes handle that, each a Reconnect: Reconnect::automatic, the default, dials again after a pause. The first pause is 100 ms, and each failed dial doubles it up to 5 seconds. AutoReconnect sets both pauses and a limit of dials; there is no limit by default. When the server reports that it no longer has the session, the task subscribes every filter again. Reconnect::never ends every subscription's stream at the first loss, and every publish fails from then on. Reconnect::custom hands the recovery to a Reconnector of the service's own. It gets why the connection ended, a dial that installs the new connection for every publisher, the open subscriptions and the helpers that subscribe them again. It decides how to dial, what to restore and when to give up. While a mode recovers, the handlers keep running and the subscriptions stay open. With a persistent session the server keeps the subscriptions and what arrived during the gap. A refusal that retrying cannot change ends the task in every mode: bad credentials, a withdrawn authorization, an unacceptable client id, a TLS handshake the certificates cannot satisfy. A mode that gives up ends the task too. Every subscription then returns the reason as MqttError::Receive, and its stream ends. The application's on_subscription_end setting decides whether the service stops. keep_alive is how long the connection may stay silent. When nothing else is sent for that long, the client pings the server. The server closes a connection it has heard nothing from for one and a half keep-alive intervals, and publishes its last will. The client notices a server that stopped answering the same way, and reconnects. The default is 60 seconds, and the client's minimum is 5: a shorter one fails startup, in a TestApp test as on a server.

A silent connection is noticed within about 15 seconds. The session outlives the gap by an hour, so what arrives while the service reconnects is kept for it. After 120 failed dials, about ten minutes, every subscription ends, and SubscriptionEnd::FailFast stops the service with an error. Macros Manual examples/mqtt_broker_reconnect.rs /// About ten minutes of dials: pauses from 100 ms up to 5 s, then every subscription ends. const ATTEMPTS: NonZeroU32 = NonZeroU32::new(120).unwrap(); /// A connection silent for 15 seconds is probed, and one that stays silent is dropped and dialed /// again. The session outlives the gap by an hour, so what arrives meanwhile is kept. fn broker(url: &str, client_id: &str) -> MqttBroker { MqttBroker::new(url, client_id) .keep_alive(Duration::from_secs(15)) .clean_start(false) .session_expiry(Duration::from_hours(1)) .reconnect(Reconnect::automatic( AutoReconnect::new().attempts(ATTEMPTS), )) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(broker("mqtt://localhost:1883", "telemetry-svc")) } examples/manual/mqtt_broker_reconnect.rs /// About ten minutes of dials: pauses from 100 ms up to 5 s, then every subscription ends. const ATTEMPTS: NonZeroU32 = NonZeroU32::new(120).unwrap(); /// A connection silent for 15 seconds is probed, and one that stays silent is dropped and dialed /// again. The session outlives the gap by an hour, so what arrives meanwhile is kept. fn broker(url: &str, client_id: &str) -> MqttBroker { MqttBroker::new(url, client_id) .keep_alive(Duration::from_secs(15)) .clean_start(false) .session_expiry(Duration::from_hours(1)) .reconnect(Reconnect::automatic( AutoReconnect::new().attempts(ATTEMPTS), )) } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(broker("mqtt://localhost:1883", "telemetry-svc")) }

This one logs in with a fresh password on every dial and gives up after a minute. A session the server did not keep gets every subscription again, in the order they were opened. Macros Manual examples/mqtt_broker_reconnect.rs /// Logs in with a fresh password on every dial, and subscribes again what a lost session took. struct FreshLogin; /// The password as the secret store holds it now, which a rotation may have changed. fn current_password() -> String { std::env::var("MQTT_PASSWORD").unwrap_or_default() } impl Reconnector for FreshLogin { async fn reconnect(&self, recovery: &mut Recovery<'_>) -> Result<Reconnected, MqttError> { tracing::warn!(reason = %recovery.lost(), "mqtt connection lost"); let mut failed = 0; let reconnected = loop { recovery.credentials("telemetry-svc", current_password()); match recovery.connect().await { Ok(reconnected) => break reconnected, Err(err) if failed == 30 => return Err(err), Err(_) => failed += 1, } tokio::time::sleep(Duration::from_secs(2)).await; }; if !reconnected.session_present() { recovery.restore_all().await?; } Ok(reconnected) } } fn custom_broker(url: &str, client_id: &str) -> MqttBroker { MqttBroker::new(url, client_id).reconnect(Reconnect::custom(FreshLogin)) } examples/manual/mqtt_broker_reconnect.rs /// Logs in with a fresh password on every dial, and subscribes again what a lost session took. struct FreshLogin; /// The password as the secret store holds it now, which a rotation may have changed. fn current_password() -> String { std::env::var("MQTT_PASSWORD").unwrap_or_default() } impl Reconnector for FreshLogin { async fn reconnect(&self, recovery: &mut Recovery<'_>) -> Result<Reconnected, MqttError> { tracing::warn!(reason = %recovery.lost(), "mqtt connection lost"); let mut failed = 0; let reconnected = loop { recovery.credentials("telemetry-svc", current_password()); match recovery.connect().await { Ok(reconnected) => break reconnected, Err(err) if failed == 30 => return Err(err), Err(_) => failed += 1, } tokio::time::sleep(Duration::from_secs(2)).await; }; if !reconnected.session_present() { recovery.restore_all().await?; } Ok(reconnected) } } fn custom_broker(url: &str, client_id: &str) -> MqttBroker { MqttBroker::new(url, client_id).reconnect(Reconnect::custom(FreshLogin)) }
documents.s: A reconnection of the service's own

documents.t: The login in the URL or credentials sends a user name and a password; tls_ca trusts a certificate authority and selects TLS, and tls_client_auth adds a client certificate. The user name and the password travel in the CONNECT packet. A server that refuses them fails startup at once, naming the refusal. A URL such as mqtt://user:password@host:1884 logs in with the user name and the password it carries. They are percent-decoded, as a URL writes them, so p%40ss is the password p@ss. The URL logs in only when it carries both a non-empty user name and a password. credentials is the explicit choice and wins over a login in the URL. TLS takes PEM bytes, so the service reads its files itself and hands their contents over. tls_ca is the certificate authority that signed the server's certificate. The client verifies the server against it and against no other store. So a TLS connection needs it: an mqtts:// URL without tls_ca fails startup, naming the missing setting. tls_ca also selects TLS on an mqtt:// URL. tls_client_auth takes the service's own certificate and key, for a server that verifies each client by its certificate, as managed MQTT services commonly do. A server may ask for both: a client certificate on a TLS listener, and a user name and a password inside the session. The login and the handshake happen on the server, so a TestApp test runs the same app in process without them. The settings are still checked as at the connect: an mqtts:// URL without tls_ca fails TestApp::start too. The generated AsyncAPI document reports the host and the port, never the credentials.

The service logs in with its user name and the password the environment gives it. Macros Manual examples/mqtt_broker_security.rs /// A server that asks every client for a user name and a password. fn password_broker(url: &str, client_id: &str, username: &str, password: &str) -> MqttBroker { MqttBroker::new(url, client_id).credentials(username, password) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { let password = env::var("MQTT_PASSWORD").unwrap_or_default(); service(password_broker( "mqtt://localhost:1884", "telemetry-svc", "telemetry-svc", &password, )) } examples/manual/mqtt_broker_security.rs /// A server that asks every client for a user name and a password. fn password_broker(url: &str, client_id: &str, username: &str, password: &str) -> MqttBroker { MqttBroker::new(url, client_id).credentials(username, password) } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { let password = env::var("MQTT_PASSWORD").unwrap_or_default(); service(password_broker( "mqtt://localhost:1884", "telemetry-svc", "telemetry-svc", &password, )) } A deployment that hands over one connection string passes it as it is. Macros Manual examples/mqtt_broker_security.rs /// The deployment hands over one connection string with the login in it, such as /// `mqtt://telemetry-svc:p%40ss@broker.internal:1884` for the password `p@ss`. fn url_broker(url: &str, client_id: &str) -> MqttBroker { MqttBroker::new(url, client_id) } examples/manual/mqtt_broker_security.rs /// The deployment hands over one connection string with the login in it, such as /// `mqtt://telemetry-svc:p%40ss@broker.internal:1884` for the password `p@ss`. fn url_broker(url: &str, client_id: &str) -> MqttBroker { MqttBroker::new(url, client_id) } On a TLS listener that verifies clients by their certificates, the service hands over the three PEM files of its deployment. Macros Manual examples/mqtt_broker_security.rs /// A TLS listener that verifies the service by its certificate. `dir` holds the PEM files the /// deployment mounts: the authority that signed the server's certificate, and the service's own /// certificate and key. fn tls_broker(url: &str, client_id: &str, dir: &Path) -> io::Result<MqttBroker> { Ok(MqttBroker::new(url, client_id) .tls_ca(fs::read(dir.join("ca.crt"))?) .tls_client_auth( fs::read(dir.join("client.crt"))?, fs::read(dir.join("client.key"))?, )) } examples/manual/mqtt_broker_security.rs /// A TLS listener that verifies the service by its certificate. `dir` holds the PEM files the /// deployment mounts: the authority that signed the server's certificate, and the service's own /// certificate and key. fn tls_broker(url: &str, client_id: &str, dir: &Path) -> io::Result<MqttBroker> { Ok(MqttBroker::new(url, client_id) .tls_ca(fs::read(dir.join("ca.crt"))?) .tls_client_auth( fs::read(dir.join("client.crt"))?, fs::read(dir.join("client.key"))?, )) }

clean_start(false) with a session_expiry keeps the session on the server, so a service that loses its connection gets what arrived meanwhile. An MQTT session belongs to a client id and lives on the server. It holds the client's subscriptions and the QoS 1 and 2 messages the client has not acknowledged yet. By default every connect starts a clean session, and the server forgets it when the connection ends. clean_start(false) asks the server to resume the session the client id already has. session_expiry says how long the server keeps it after the connection ends. The duration counts in whole seconds, and anything longer than u32::MAX seconds keeps the session with no end. Without an expiry the server drops the session with the connection, whatever clean_start says. While the session lives, the server queues every QoS 1 and 2 message that matches its subscriptions. When the service connects again under the same id, the server sends what it queued, then what arrives next. This covers a lost connection, a reconnect, a process that dies and a clean shutdown. A clean shutdown leaves the app's subscriptions in the session, so a service that restarts receives what was published while it was stopped. A QoS 0 message is never queued. A delivery the handler left unacknowledged, such as one HandlerOutcome::retry() settled, comes back when the session resumes. The session lives on the server, so a TestApp test in process starts a fresh one every time. What a session keeps is for a live test.

The server keeps the service's session for a day. A reading published while the service is down reaches it when it comes back. Macros Manual examples/mqtt_broker_session.rs /// The server at `url` keeps this client's session for a day after the service disconnects. fn broker(url: &str, client_id: &str) -> MqttBroker { MqttBroker::new(url, client_id) .clean_start(false) .session_expiry(Duration::from_hours(24)) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(broker("mqtt://localhost:1883", "telemetry-svc")) } examples/manual/mqtt_broker_session.rs /// The server at `url` keeps this client's session for a day after the service disconnects. fn broker(url: &str, client_id: &str) -> MqttBroker { MqttBroker::new(url, client_id) .clean_start(false) .session_expiry(Duration::from_hours(24)) } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(broker("mqtt://localhost:1883", "telemetry-svc")) }

Shutdown sends a clean DISCONNECT and waits up to 5 s for what is queued to leave; a publisher used afterwards reports MqttError::NotConnected. The runtime stops reading first and lets the handlers in flight finish. How long they get is the app's shutdown_timeout, with no bound by default. Their publishes and acknowledgements join the client's queue as they settle. Each subscription leaves its filter on the server as it closes, so a persistent session keeps the app's subscriptions, and the server queues what arrives until the service returns. Then the broker sends a DISCONNECT behind everything already queued. It waits up to 5 seconds for the connection task to write the queue out, and logs a warning when they run out. The server discards the last will of a connection that ends this way. A publisher taken before the shutdown keeps pointing at the closed connection. A publish through it returns MqttError::NotConnected and never succeeds against the dead connection. An acknowledgement after the shutdown is refused too.

The handlers get ten seconds to finish, and their alerts leave before the broker disconnects. Macros Manual examples/mqtt_broker_shutdown.rs /// At shutdown the handlers get ten seconds to finish; their alerts and acknowledgements leave /// before the broker disconnects. fn service(broker: MqttBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("telemetry", "0.1.0")) .shutdown_timeout(Duration::from_secs(10)) .with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(check) .out(DefaultSlot, Publish::default()) .build(); }) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(MqttBroker::new("mqtt://localhost:1883", "telemetry-svc")) } examples/manual/mqtt_broker_shutdown.rs /// At shutdown the handlers get ten seconds to finish; their alerts and acknowledgements leave /// before the broker disconnects. fn service(broker: MqttBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("telemetry", "0.1.0")) .shutdown_timeout(Duration::from_secs(10)) .with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(subscriber("broker-shutdown/telemetry", Check).build()) .out(DefaultSlot, Publish::default()) .build(); }) } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(MqttBroker::new("mqtt://localhost:1883", "telemetry-svc")) }

Startup waits up to 30 seconds for the server's CONNACK; a refusal the connection cannot outgrow fails it at once, naming the cause. The runtime connects the broker first. The settings are checked before anything is dialed: a keep-alive under five seconds, an mqtts:// URL without tls_ca or a port that is not a number fail startup with MqttError::Invalid. Then the connection task dials the server. A server that is down or busy is dialed again with a backoff, until it answers or the 30 seconds run out. A timeout fails startup with MqttError::Connect, and the error carries the last reason a dial failed. Some refusals give the same answer on every attempt: wrong credentials, a client id the server rejects, a peer that is not an MQTT server, and a TLS handshake the certificates cannot satisfy. Each fails startup at once with MqttError::Connect, naming the refusal. A server that refuses a client certificate after the handshake answers the way a broken connection does, so that refusal is retried and reported when the 30 seconds run out. Once connected, the runtime opens every subscription, each one waiting for the server's SUBACK. A filter the server rejects fails startup with MqttError::Subscribe. The after_startup hooks run last, so a hook publishes through a connection whose subscriptions are already open. A TestApp test in process checks the settings as the connect does, then opens the subscriptions and runs the hooks. The dial and the server's refusals are for a live test.

Once its subscriptions are open, the service announces that it is online on its status topic. The announcement is retained, so a dashboard that subscribes later reads it. Macros Manual examples/mqtt_broker_startup.rs /// Once the connection is up and every subscription is open, the service announces itself on its /// status topic, retained for whoever subscribes later. fn service(broker: MqttBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("telemetry", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(record); b.after_startup( Publish::default().retain(true), async move |publisher| -> Result<(), PublishError<MqttError>> { publisher.message(&Status { online: true }).publish().await }, ); }) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(MqttBroker::new("mqtt://localhost:1883", "telemetry-svc")) } examples/manual/mqtt_broker_startup.rs /// Once the connection is up and every subscription is open, the service announces itself on its /// status topic, retained for whoever subscribes later. fn service(broker: MqttBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("telemetry", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(subscriber("broker-startup/telemetry", Record).build()); b.after_startup( Publish::default().retain(true), async move |publisher| -> Result<(), PublishError<MqttError>> { publisher.message(&Status { online: true }).publish().await }, ); }) } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(MqttBroker::new("mqtt://localhost:1883", "telemetry-svc")) }

Ctx<DeliveryTopic> gives a handler the topic a message was published to, which differs from the filter that matched it. MqttContext is what a delivery carries besides its payload and headers. The subscription builds it once per delivery. It holds one field, the topic, under the key DeliveryTopic. Both are in the prelude. A handler binds the topic as a parameter with Ctx<DeliveryTopic>, which hands it over as a String. A body that takes ctx: &mut Context<'_, MqttContext> reads it borrowed with ctx.context(DeliveryTopic), as the manual form does. On an MqttFilter the topic tells the messages of the filter apart: devices/dev42/telemetry and devices/dev43/telemetry both match devices/+/telemetry. The subscription's name, ctx.name(), is the filter, never the topic. The same key reads the topic in a publish transform on the reply or the retry position, through cx.context(DeliveryTopic); a transform on the retry position sends a copy back to the topic its delivery arrived on.

An alarm names no device; the topic it arrived on does. Macros Manual examples/mqtt_context.rs /// The alarm itself names no device: its topic does, at the level the filter's `+` matched. #[subscriber(MqttFilter::new("devices/+/alarms"), reply)] async fn open_incident(alarm: &Alarm, Ctx(topic): Ctx<DeliveryTopic>) -> Incident { let device = topic.split('/').nth(1).unwrap_or_default().to_owned(); tracing::info!(%topic, alarm.code, "incident opened"); Incident { device, code: alarm.code, } } examples/manual/mqtt_context.rs /// The alarm itself names no device: its topic does, at the level the filter's `+` matched. struct OpenIncident; impl Handle<Alarm, Incident, (), MqttContext> for OpenIncident { fn handle( &self, alarm: &Alarm, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, MqttContext>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Incident, HandlerOutcome>> { let topic = ctx.context(DeliveryTopic); let device = topic.split('/').nth(1).unwrap_or_default().to_owned(); tracing::info!(%topic, alarm.code, "incident opened"); ready(Ok(Incident { device, code: alarm.code, })) } }

MqttPublish, Publish in the prelude, sets the QoS and the retain flag; a publish returns once the client session owns the message. A PUBLISH packet carries two arguments besides the topic: a quality of service and the retain flag. The policy declares both: qos defaults to Qos::AtLeastOnce, and retain to false. A mount site names it wherever a registration publishes: .out_reply(Publish::default()) for a reply, .out(Slot, Publish::default()) for a slot, .out_retry(Publish::default()) for retry copies. A scope's after_startup hook takes one too, for a message the service sends once it is connected. The policy holds no connection; the runtime pairs it with the connected broker at startup into an MqttPublisher. A reply mounted without a policy sends through Publish::default(), to the topic its type declares. A publish returns once the client session owns the message, not once the server confirmed it. At QoS 1 and 2 the session sends the message again until the server acknowledges it, across reconnects. A topic with a + or # wildcard is refused with MqttError::Publish. One message changes the arguments with the qos and retain steps.

Headers travel as MQTT 5 user properties; content-type, reply-to and correlation-id take the protocol's own properties. A peer in any language reads them as plain MQTT, with no envelope around the payload. content-type becomes the content type property, reply-to the response topic a responder answers on, and correlation-id the correlation data, in both directions. A message with no headers is published with no properties at all. A textual content type (application/json, any text/ type, any +json type) sets the payload format indicator to 1, which tells a peer the body is UTF-8; any other sets it to 0. A property is an MQTT string, and a server may close the connection on one with a control character. So a header name or value that is not UTF-8, or carries a control character or a Unicode non-character, refuses the publish with MqttError::Publish. The codec of a position writes no header, so nothing sets the content type unless the service does. A publish transform sets it at the mount site, once for every message of one position: the replies, a slot or the retry copies.

The qos and retain steps change one message's QoS or retain flag over the policy; a handler bounds its slot with MqttPublishOptions. MqttPublishSteps puts both steps on the publish builder, in any order. An argument the call does not name keeps what the policy declared at the mount site. The values reach the client as the protocol fields they are, so a subscriber receives a plain message with no extra property. A publish with no call site of its own, a reply or a retry copy, takes the policy whole. The steps are reached from a slot whose bound names the options type: Out<impl Publisher<Options = MqttPublishOptions>, Slot>. That bound and this crate's prelude are the one place a handler body names the broker. A test reads what the steps set with tb.out::<Slot>().with_options(&MqttPublishOptions::default().retain(true)).

A responder answers on the response topic a request carries, through a reply transform that also copies the correlation data. An MQTT 5 request carries the topic its answer goes to in the response topic property, and the handler reads it as the reply-to header. Its correlation data arrives as the correlation-id header, and the requester matches the answer to its question by it. A PublishTransform on the reply position reads both from the request: cx.headers().reply_to() and cx.headers().correlation_id(). It names the answer's topic, so it declares type Destination = Names. The reply type declares no topic of its own, which is what leaves the naming to the transform. The topic the mount site names, reply("..") in the macro form, is the fallback: a request without a response topic is answered there. The generated document points the reply's address at the request's reply-to header, as Replies shows.

A retained message stays on its topic for every later subscriber of a matching filter; an empty retained payload clears it. The server keeps the last retained message of each topic. A subscription that opens later receives it at once, so a dashboard that starts after a device announced its state still reads that state. A publisher retains every message with Publish::default().retain(true), and one message with the retain step. Publishing an empty payload retained removes the message the server kept for that topic. A shared subscription receives no retained messages. A scope's after_startup hook runs once the broker is connected, which is where a service announces its own status. A state is bytes on the wire rather than an encoded model, so its type carries its own bytes with #[derive(Serialized)], and no codec runs on them.

An ack sends PUBACK at QoS 1 and PUBREC at QoS 2; QoS 0 has no acknowledgement, and MQTT has no negative one. A message settles when the handler returns, and the delivery's own quality of service decides what that sends. A delivery arrives at the lower of the publisher's QoS and the subscription's, so a QoS 1 subscription still receives a QoS 0 publish at QoS 0. At QoS 1 and 2 the server keeps a delivery until it is acknowledged; the client finishes the QoS 2 handshake on its own. A QoS 0 delivery has no acknowledgement packet, so settling it reports AckError::Unsupported, which the runtime logs as a warning. drop acknowledges the delivery too, because an acknowledgement is the only final answer MQTT has; the server never sends the message again. retry asks for a negative acknowledgement, which MQTT does not have, so the delivery stays unacknowledged. retry_after is the outcome that retries within the session. In the manual form Ok acknowledges and Err(outcome) settles by the outcome. When the server sends one packet for two overlapping filters, the acknowledgement belongs to one delivery, and settling the other reports Unsupported.

dead_letter(topic) names the topic a delivery that reached its cap is published to; it lies outside every filter the service reads. It follows max_attempts(n) at the mount site. When the n-th delivery asks for a retry, the runtime acknowledges it and publishes it to the dead-letter topic instead. The message keeps its payload and its headers. RETRY_COUNT_HEADER on it says how many times it was delivered. The dead-letter topic is an ordinary topic, and a subscription of this service or of another one reads it. A filter of the service that matches the dead-letter topic receives the spent message as a new delivery, so the topic stays outside every other filter the service reads.

A filter subscription names where its retry copies go, once with out_retry(..).to(..) or per delivery with a transform. An MqttTopic reads one topic, and its copies go there; a share group's copies go to the plain topic, not to $share/... An MqttFilter matches many topics and is a topic of its own only by accident, so the mount site names the destination. out_retry binds the Retry slot, the one the runtime publishes its copies through, to a publish policy. .to(topic) sends every copy to one topic; a topic the filter matches brings the copies back to the same handler. A publish transform that declares Names picks the topic per delivery instead, such as the topic the delivery arrived on. It reads that topic from the MqttContext of the delivery, which reaches the slot when the handler reads it: a Ctx<DeliveryTopic> parameter, or a manual body typed over MqttContext. Naming a topic and adding a naming transform are mutually exclusive, and writing both does not compile. A filter registration that names neither does not start, and the error names the subscription. The copy carries the delivery's own bytes, so a codec on the slot encodes nothing, while a transform still runs.

max_attempts(n) caps the deliveries one message gets, counted on the retry-count header, because MQTT counts no redeliveries. A redelivered PUBLISH packet carries a duplicate flag and no counter. So the runtime counts on RETRY_COUNT_HEADER, which travels on the copies retry_after publishes. The cap counts deliveries, the first one included: nonzero!(5u32) gives a message five. Under a cap every retry travels as such a copy, an immediate retry() too, so the count reaches the cap whichever outcome the handler returns. The delivery that reaches the cap goes to the dead-letter topic instead of coming back. A cap without a dead-letter topic rejects the delivery, which on MQTT acknowledges it and lets it go; a warning names the subscription. A filter subscription also names where its copies go, with out_retry.

retry_after(delay) acknowledges the delivery, waits, then publishes a copy of the message with its retry count in a header. MQTT holds no message back and counts no deliveries, so the runtime does both. It acknowledges the original, waits out the delay and publishes the payload and the headers as they arrived. The copy carries RETRY_COUNT_HEADER, raised by one on every copy, and the handler reads it like any other header. An MqttTopic subscription receives its copies on its own topic; an MqttFilter names where they go with out_retry. The copy waits in the service's memory, so a process that exits before the delay is over loses it. A QoS 0 delivery has no acknowledgement, and its copy is published all the same. A copy is an ordinary publish, so every subscription whose filter matches its topic receives it, in this service and in any other. A retried topic therefore lies outside every other filter the service reads, or another handler reads the copy too. max_attempts caps the deliveries of one message.

A reading the database timed out on is written again five seconds later. retry() leaves a delivery unacknowledged: it comes back when a persistent session resumes, never within the connection. The outcome asks the broker for a negative acknowledgement, and MQTT has none. The runtime logs the refusal and moves on, and nothing acknowledges the delivery later. At QoS 1 and 2 the server keeps the message in the client's session. It sends the message again when the service connects with the same client id and the session is still there: clean_start(false) and a session_expiry longer than the gap. With a clean start, or once the session expired, the message is gone; at QoS 0 it is gone at once. Until the connection ends, the delivery holds one slot of the receive_maximum window, 1000 by default. When the window is full of unacknowledged deliveries, the server sends no more QoS 1 or 2 messages on that connection. For a retry within the session, a handler returns retry_after. A registration with a cap turns retry() into an immediate copy of the message instead.

A topic in #[subscriber] subscribes to that one topic at QoS 1; a descriptor carries wildcards, the quality of service and a share group. #[subscriber("devices/dev42/telemetry")] subscribes to the topic devices/dev42/telemetry. The bare name is an MqttTopic with its defaults: Qos::AtLeastOnce and no share group. A name with a + or # wildcard is a filter, not a topic, so the service does not start, and the error names MqttFilter, the descriptor that takes it. Every other setting belongs to a descriptor: MqttTopic for one topic, MqttFilter for a filter with wildcards. Each descriptor carries its quality of service and its share group. A descriptor goes where the name goes, as the attribute's first argument. The manual form passes the name to subscriber(name, body), and a descriptor joins the chain through map_source. The subscription is open once the server has acknowledged it, before the service takes its first message.

A slice handler reads batches the crate assembles on the client: a batch closes at the size the mount site names or 20 ms after its first delivery. A handler over &[T] is a batch handler, and batch(n) at the mount site is its largest batch. An MQTT packet carries one message, so the crate collects deliveries into batches on the client. A batch closes when it holds n deliveries, or 20 milliseconds after its first delivery, whichever comes first. The size is the mount site's, and the 20 ms deadline is the crate's. A subscription with nothing to read waits for its first delivery as long as it takes. Nothing at the mount site says which side of the wire filled a batch, so a batch handler written for another broker mounts here unchanged. One outcome settles every delivery of the batch, and a Vec<HandlerOutcome> settles delivery i with outcome i. Each delivery is acknowledged on its own. A batch abandoned while it fills leaves its deliveries unacknowledged. In the manual form the body is an impl Handle<[T]>, where Ok(()) acks the batch and Err(outcomes) settles delivery by delivery.

workers(n, by_key) keeps deliveries that share the partition-key header on one lane, in order, while other keys run in parallel. workers(n, by_key) runs n sequential lanes over one subscription. The lane of a delivery is picked by a hash of its partition key, so deliveries with one key run one after another, in the order they arrived. Deliveries with different keys run at once on different lanes. A delivery without a key goes to the next lane in rotation and keeps no order with any other. MQTT has no partitions, so the key is the header PARTITION_KEY_HEADER, partition-key, which travels as an MQTT 5 user property. The protocol gives the property no meaning: it is a convention between the publisher, which sets it, and this crate, which reads it back. A service that publishes to a keyed subscription sets the header on each message, such as the tenant or the device the message belongs to. The lanes order work inside one connection. A share group spreads messages over instances and keeps no order by key between them. The manual form writes the lanes as .workers_by_key(n) on the mount chain.

The checkout keys each order by its tenant. Orders of one tenant run in order on one lane, and different tenants run side by side. b.include(checkout) .out(DefaultSlot, Publish::default()) .build(); }, ) } examples/manual/mqtt_subscriptions_lanes.rs use ruststream_rumqttc::PARTITION_KEY_HEADER; use ruststream_rumqttc::prelude::*; MqttFilter subscribes with the + and # wildcards; each delivery carries its own topic, and the mount site names where retry copies go. MqttFilter::new takes the topic filter. + matches exactly one level of a topic, and # matches every level that remains, so it may only come last. A filter that starts with a wildcard does not match a topic that starts with $, such as the server's own $SYS topics. qos sets the quality of service, and shared puts the subscription in a share group. The subscription's name is the filter. A handler reads the topic each message was published to through DeliveryTopic. A filter with # before its last level, or one with a control character, stops the service at startup. A filter is no topic a publisher can use, so the subscription has no topic of its own for a retry_after copy. The mount site names one with .out_retry(policy).to(topic), or names one per delivery with a transform. A registration that names neither does not start, and the error names the subscription and MqttFilter. A destination the filter matches brings the copy back to this subscription.

MqttTopic subscribes to one topic with no wildcard, so a retry copy published to that topic comes back with nothing named at the mount site. MqttTopic::new takes the topic. qos sets the quality of service, AtLeastOnce by default. shared puts the subscription in a share group. The subscription's name is the topic: a test reads its deliveries under that name, and the topic is the channel of the AsyncAPI document. A topic is also a name a publisher can use. So a retry_after copy is published to the subscription's own topic, and the mount site names no destination for it. The copy is an ordinary publish, so every subscription whose filter matches the topic receives it too. A share group does not change where the copy goes: it is published to the plain topic. An empty topic, a topic with a + or # wildcard, or one with a control character stops the service at startup, before anything is subscribed. A wildcard belongs to MqttFilter, and the error names it.

Commands for one valve, read at QoS 2; a command the valve refuses comes back five seconds later. Macros Manual examples/mqtt_subscriptions_topic.rs /// Runs the commands sent to dev42; the valve refuses the first attempt while it settles, so the /// command comes back as a copy five seconds later. #[subscriber(MqttTopic::new("devices/dev42/commands").qos(Qos::ExactlyOnce))] async fn execute(command: &Command, ctx: &mut Context) -> HandlerOutcome { if ctx.headers().get_str(RETRY_COUNT_HEADER).is_none() { tracing::info!(command.id, "valve settling, trying again"); return HandlerOutcome::retry_after(SETTLE); } tracing::info!(command.id, command.open, "command executed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("valves", "0.1.0")).with_broker( MqttBroker::new("mqtt://localhost:1883", "valves-svc"), |b| { // The topic is where a copy goes, so the mount site names nothing. b.include(execute); }, ) } examples/manual/mqtt_subscriptions_topic.rs /// Runs the commands sent to dev42; the valve refuses the first attempt while it settles, so the /// command comes back as a copy five seconds later. struct Execute; impl Handle<Command> for Execute { fn handle( &self, command: &Command, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if ctx.headers().get_str(RETRY_COUNT_HEADER).is_none() { tracing::info!(command.id, "valve settling, trying again"); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(SETTLE))); } tracing::info!(command.id, command.open, "command executed"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("valves", "0.1.0")).with_broker( MqttBroker::new("mqtt://localhost:1883", "valves-svc"), |b| { let commands = MqttTopic::new("devices/dev42/commands").qos(Qos::ExactlyOnce); // The topic is where a copy goes, so the mount site names nothing. b.include( subscriber("devices/dev42/commands", Execute) .build() .map_source(|_| commands), ); }, ) }

Overlapping filters on one connection each receive a message once, told apart by subscription identifiers; one filter mounted twice shares it. Two filters overlap when one topic can match both, such as devices/+/telemetry and devices/dev42/#. They are two subscriptions to the server, and each receives a message once. The server sends a packet per matching subscription, and the crate tells the packets apart by MQTT 5 subscription identifiers. The crate attaches an identifier only to a filter that meets another one on the same connection. A share group next to a plain subscription on the same filter overlaps the same way. The same filter mounted twice, or two members of one share group, is one subscription to the server. The crate hands its deliveries to the mounts in turn, and the filter stays subscribed while any of them is open. A shutdown leaves it in the session. A server announces whether it offers subscription identifiers when the connection opens. On a server without them, a filter that meets another one on the same connection does not open, and the error names both filters. Two brokers with client ids of their own keep such filters on separate connections.

The fleet's readings and everything dev42 sends: a reading of dev42 reaches both handlers, once each. Each retry topic matches its own filter only, so a retry copy returns to the subscription that asked for it. Macros Manual examples/mqtt_subscriptions_overlaps.rs /// Records the readings of the whole fleet. #[subscriber(MqttFilter::new("devices/+/telemetry"))] async fn record(telemetry: &Telemetry) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(device = %telemetry.device, telemetry.temperature, "reading recorded"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// Watches everything dev42 sends, its readings included. #[subscriber(MqttFilter::new("devices/dev42/#"))] async fn watch(telemetry: &Telemetry) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(device = %telemetry.device, "dev42 watched"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("telemetry", "0.1.0")).with_broker( MqttBroker::new("mqtt://localhost:1883", "telemetry-svc"), |b| { // Each retry topic matches its own filter and not the other one, so a copy comes // back to the subscription that asked for it alone. b.include(record) .out_retry(Publish::default()) .to("devices/retry/telemetry"); b.include(watch) .out_retry(Publish::default()) .to("devices/dev42/retry"); }, ) } examples/manual/mqtt_subscriptions_overlaps.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("telemetry", "0.1.0")).with_broker( MqttBroker::new("mqtt://localhost:1883", "telemetry-svc"), |b| { // Each retry topic matches its own filter and not the other one, so a copy comes // back to the subscription that asked for it alone. b.include( subscriber("devices/+/telemetry", Record) .build() .map_source(|_| MqttFilter::new("devices/+/telemetry")), ) .out_retry(Publish::default()) .to("devices/retry/telemetry"); b.include( subscriber("devices/dev42/#", Watch) .build() .map_source(|_| MqttFilter::new("devices/dev42/#")), ) .out_retry(Publish::default()) .to("devices/dev42/retry"); }, ) }

Qos picks at most once, at least once or exactly once; a delivery arrives at the lower of the publisher's and the subscription's level. A subscription names its level with qos(..) on MqttTopic or MqttFilter. The default is Qos::AtLeastOnce. Level QoS What the protocol does AtMostOnce 0 sends the message once, with no acknowledgement; a message lost on the way is gone AtLeastOnce 1 resends until the receiver answers PUBACK; a message may arrive twice ExactlyOnce 2 a four-packet handshake, so the message arrives once The server sends each message at the lower of two levels: the one its publisher sent it at and the one the subscription asked for. So a QoS 2 subscription receives a QoS 0 publish at QoS 0. A delivery at QoS 1 or 2 is acknowledged when the handler settles it. A delivery at QoS 0 has no acknowledgement packet, so settling it reports AckError::Unsupported. The level a publish is sent at is a setting of the publish policy.

Telemetry read at most once, because the next reading replaces a lost one, and valve commands read exactly once. Macros Manual examples/mqtt_subscriptions_qos.rs /// A device reports every few seconds, so a lost reading costs nothing: at most once. #[subscriber(MqttFilter::new("devices/+/telemetry").qos(Qos::AtMostOnce))] async fn sample(telemetry: &Telemetry) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(device = %telemetry.device, telemetry.temperature, "reading sampled"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// A valve command must run once and never twice: exactly once. #[subscriber(MqttTopic::new("devices/dev42/commands").qos(Qos::ExactlyOnce))] async fn execute(command: &Command) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(command.id, command.open, "command executed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/mqtt_subscriptions_qos.rs /// A device reports every few seconds, so a lost reading costs nothing: at most once. fn readings() -> MqttFilter { MqttFilter::new("devices/+/telemetry").qos(Qos::AtMostOnce) } /// A valve command must run once and never twice: exactly once. fn commands() -> MqttTopic { MqttTopic::new("devices/dev42/commands").qos(Qos::ExactlyOnce) }

shared(group) makes a share group: the server hands each message to one member, and retained messages reach none of them. A share group is how MQTT 5 spreads messages over competing consumers. MqttFilter::new("devices/+/telemetry").shared("workers") subscribes $share/workers/devices/+/telemetry. MqttTopic::shared does the same for one topic. Every instance of a service that subscribes with the same group and the same filter is a member, and the server sends each message to one member only. A subscription outside the group on the same filter still receives every message. The group belongs to the subscribed filter alone. The subscription's name, the delivery's topic and the destination of a retry copy stay the plain form. A retained message is not sent to a share group. An empty group name, or one with /, + or #, stops the service at startup. Two members of one group on one connection are one subscription to the server, and the crate hands their deliveries out in turn.

Each instance of the telemetry service joins workers, so the fleet's readings are spread over the instances. Macros Manual examples/mqtt_subscriptions_shared.rs /// Every instance of the service joins the group `workers`, so each reading is handled once. #[subscriber(MqttFilter::new("devices/+/telemetry").shared("workers"))] async fn process(telemetry: &Telemetry) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(device = %telemetry.device, telemetry.temperature, "reading processed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/mqtt_subscriptions_shared.rs /// Every instance of the service joins the group `workers`, so each reading is handled once. fn fleet() -> MqttFilter { MqttFilter::new("devices/+/telemetry").shared("workers") }

TestApp::start runs the production app on an in-process MQTT server: wildcards, share groups, retained messages and QoS, with no broker. A test hands the harness the app main runs, unchanged, and addresses the broker by its production type, tb.broker::<MqttBroker>(). The testing feature in [dev-dependencies] adds the in-process mode, and turns on the core's harness with it. The in-process server has no settings of its own. It reads the broker's, and checks them as the connect does: a keep-alive under five seconds or an mqtts:// URL without tls_ca fails TestApp::start. A publish goes through the same validation and the same mapping onto MQTT 5 properties as on the wire. It routes as a server routes. A publish reaches every subscription whose filter matches its topic, + and # included, and a filter starting with a wildcard skips the topics that start with $. A share group hands each message to one of its members. Two overlapping filters each receive their own copy, as a server sends them. A delivery arrives at the lower of the publish and the subscription QoS, and a QoS 0 delivery has nothing to acknowledge. A retained message reaches every later subscription outside a share group, and an empty retained payload clears it. A message over the broker's max_packet_size never arrives, and a publish or an acknowledgement after shutdown is refused. A publish through the harness returns once every handler it woke has settled, a reply included. The assertions that follow read finished state. What only a server has is for a live test: the login and TLS, a persistent session, the last will, the receive window, a lost connection, and several connections on one server.

The dependency line: [dev-dependencies] ruststream-rumqttc = { version = "0.7", features = ["testing"] } The test publishes a hot reading to one device's topic, and reads how the handler settled it and the alert it published. TestApp::start_live runs the same test body against a running MQTT server, for what only a server has: sessions, the last will, flow control. It connects the broker through its ordinary connect, so startup waits for the server's CONNACK and each subscription for its SUBACK. The body is the one an in-process test runs; only the start call differs. A publish, settle and advance wait on the real clock until every subscription has handled what was published to it. The wait lasts ten seconds at most, and start_live_within sets another bound. The live mode is for what the in-process server leaves out: the login and TLS, a persistent session, the last will, the receive window, a lost connection, and several connections sharing one server. A server is shared with whatever else runs against it. So each run connects under a client id of its own: a second connection under one id takes the session over. In the example, live::url returns the server's address from MQTT_TEST_URL, and the test returns early without one, so cargo test passes on a machine with no server. A job that stood a server up sets RUSTSTREAM_REQUIRE_LIVE=1, and a missing address then fails the test instead of skipping it. The repository's stand is a Mosquitto container in docker-compose.test.yml, which just brokers-up starts, with a listener that asks for a password and one that speaks TLS.

The two tests share one body: one in process, one against the server at MQTT_TEST_URL.
